questions.question: Profit rose from ₹-15.35 crore in FY24 to ₹29.11 crore in FY26, but only 62% of operating profit came in as cash. What does that suggest?

choices.text: The business is doing brilliantly; cash doesn't matter.
Some profit may be stuck in unpaid bills or unsold goods, so check how fast customers pay.
The company must have paid a big dividend.
Profit and cash are always equal, so the figures must be wrong.

questions.explanation: Profit is counted when a sale is made; cash arrives when the customer pays. For Foodlink F&B Holdings (India) Limited, only 62% of operating profit turned into cash, so money is getting stuck. Trade receivables and inventory are where to look.

questions.question: 46.8% of this IPO's money is an offer for sale. Where does that part of the money go?

choices.text: Into the company, to build new factories.
To the existing owners who are selling their shares.

questions.explanation: In an offer for sale, existing owners sell shares they already hold, so the money goes to them. Only the fresh issue, ₹192 crore here, reaches Foodlink F&B Holdings (India) Limited.

questions.question: Sales went from ₹377.19 crore in FY24 to ₹567.50 crore in FY26, which is 22.7% a year. How would you describe that?
questions.explanation: 22.7% a year is healthy growth: Foodlink F&B Holdings (India) Limited's customers are buying more each year.

questions.question: Foodlink F&B Holdings (India) Limited owes 0.11 rupees of loans for every rupee of its owners' money. Which is closest to the truth?

choices.text: Its loans are small to manageable next to what the owners have put in.
Its loans are heavy: lenders have more riding on it than its owners.
Loans never matter for a company that makes a profit.

questions.explanation: At 0.11 rupees of loans per rupee of owners' money, Foodlink F&B Holdings (India) Limited's owners have more in the business than its lenders.
